 INTRODUCTION
 The appellant StXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX was ordered deported on February 18, 1999. An appeal has been filed from that decision.
1 The removal order was issued because the appellant was convicted of impaired driving causing death, and impaired driving causing bodily harm, offences for which a term of imprisonment of five years or more may be imposed.
2 The appellant did not contest the validity of the removal order but argued that having regard to all the circumstances of the case, he should not be removed from Canada. SUBSTANTIVE ISSUES
 Having regard to all the circumstances of the case, should the appellant not be removed from Canada? 
 
 
1 Section 70(1) of the Immigration Act Subject to subsections (4) and (5), where a removal order or conditional removal order is made against a permanent resident or against a person lawfully in possession of a valid returning resident permit issued to that person pursuant to the regulations, that person may appeal to the Appeal Division on either or both of the following grounds, namely, (a) on any ground of appeal that involves a question of law or fact, or mixed law and fact; and (b) on the ground that, having regard to all the circumstances of the case, the person should not be removed from Canada. 
2 Section 27(1) of the Immigration Act An immigration officer or a peace officer shall forward a written report to the Deputy Minister setting out the details of any information in the possession of the immigration officer or peace officer indicating that a permanent resident is a person who... (d) has been convicted of an offence under any Act of Parliament, other than an offence designated as a contravention under the Contraventions Act, for which a term of imprisonment of more than six months has been, or five years or more may be, imposed;

T99-05222 
 2DECISION
 The removal order is valid in law. The panel concluded that the execution of the removal order should be stayed for a period of five years on terms and conditions. FINDINGS OF FACT AND ANALYSIS
 The appellant came to Canada from England in 1987 at the age of 28. He is a research scientist who has worked and taught in Canada. He is also an alcoholic. The appellant has only had one incident giving rise to criminal convictions. Tragically, it was the death of his own infant son, and the injury of his other son, in a car crash caused by the appellant's impaired driving. His blood alcohol level was close to four times the legal limit. He had been secretly drinking the entire day while he and his sons were visiting friends. The appellant was initially given a conditional sentence, during which he was under house arrest. He was permitted to leave his house to attend work, and had to seek permission to leave his home for any other purpose. On appeal, the appellant was sentenced to 19 months incarceration. He was prohibited from driving for three years. Factors to be taken into account include those set out by the Federal Court of Appeal in the decision in XXXXX
:3 
Even though this Court finds that the IRB(AD) may not consider the country conditions in a country to which a person may be deported, decisions made under the equitable jurisdiction of the IRB(AD) may, indeed must, consider broadly all the circumstances of the case in order to determine whether the deportation order was properly and equitably made. These considerations may include but would not be limited to such matters as: The seriousness of the offence leading to deportation; The possibility of rehabilitation (if a crime is involved); The impact of the crime (if crime is involved) on the victim; The remorsefulness of the applicant (if crime is involved); 
 
3 Chieu v. Canada (M.C.I.) , [1999] 1 F.C. 605 (C.A.) 
1999 CanLII 14707 (CA IRB)
T99-05222 
 3
The length of time spent in Canada and the degree to which the appellant is established here; The presence of family in Canada and the impact on it that deportation would cause; Efforts of the applicant to establish himself or herself in Canada, including employment and education; and, Support available to the applicant, not only within the family but within the community. 
 These factors are not exhaustive and the weight given to each of them will vary depending on the circumstances. In the instant case, much of the evidence applies to more than one of the areas outlined above. The offences of which the appellant was convicted are very serious. The combination of alcohol and cars is deadly, as proven by the appellant. With regard to remorse, the panel accepts that the appellant was sincere in his protestations to the panel that he is sorry for his actions. However, the panel has some concerns about the long-term prospects for the appellant's rehabilitation. He has already suffered one relapse
4 when he drank in public and drank in private, and hid the fact from his parole officer until it was about to be disclosed through other sources. Two medical reports
5 tendered on behalf of the appellant fail to refer to the relapse in May 1998, and the appellant admitted that he may not have mentioned the incident. The appellant has been very deceptive in the past about his drinking problem. His first wife was a family physician. She encouraged him to get help. He did, but refused to follow the advice. She separated from him, taking their two sons. The car crash occurred on the first weekend that she permitted her sons to be with the appellant overnight. 
 
4 Exhibit R-1, Pre-Parole Report dated 27/11/98 at p.012. 
5 Exhibit A-1, tab 1 Report of Dr. XXXXXXXXX dated August 11, 1999 and tab 4 Report of XXXXXXXXXXXXXX for the period October 19, 1998 to November 20, 1998.

T99-05222 
 4The appellant's first wife continues to be concerned about the appellant's deceptive behaviour.
6 She requires him to take breathalyser tests before visiting with his remaining son. The appellant's first wife and her son now reside in Sherbrooke, Quebec. The appellant plans to accept a position in Guelph, Ontario. He plans to make monthly trips to visit his remaining son by car. His new wife will drive. Although the appellant has completed rehabilitation programs while incarcerated, and although there have been glowing reports tendered from prison authorities, including several who testified on the appellant's behalf, the panel is concerned about the pattern of deceptive behaviour established in the past. The key element to the decision to grant a stay was the appellant's consent to the condition that he not apply for a driver's licence or own or operate an automobile for the period of the stay. Without this term, and the panel's conclusion that it is satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the appellant will honour this term, the panel would not have granted a stay, and would have dismissed the appeal. The panel is of the view that it is more likely than not that the appellant will return to his pattern of alcohol abuse, and that he will hide this from his new wife. She admitted that she had not recognized in the past how extensive his intake of alcohol had been. I find it is unlikely that she would do so in the future. The appellant plans to make the lengthy trip each month to Quebec to visit his son. This will add more incentive for him to get behind the wheel of a car. In the absence of a blanket condition preventing him from driving, the panel has concerns that he would once again combine drinking with driving. This concern is addressed by the term that the appellant not operate an automobile. In addition, the panel is satisfied that the 
 
6 Exhibit R-1, Pre-Parole Report, p.012. 
1999 CanLII 14707 (CA IRB)
T99-05222 
 5appellant's new wife will support the appellant in honouring this term. The panel accepts that the appellant's new wife would suffer hardship if the appellant were to be deported. The panel has also considered the best interests of the appellant's son, but notes the peculiar circumstances in that the appellant's behaviour in the past has put his own child in grave danger, and that without a prohibition on his ability to drive there is no guarantee that he will not do so again in the future. His first wife's requirement that he take a breathalyser before exercising access meets some of those concerns, but they are initiated by the mother of his surviving child, and not the appellant. Having reviewed all of the evidence, and giving particular weight to the appellant's agreement to the condition that he not apply for a driver's licence or own or operate an automobile during the period of the stay, and in view of the hardship which would be suffered by the appellant's new wife and by his surviving child, and after having heard the testimony of the prison officials who appeared on behalf of the appellant, and his obvious establishment in Canada, the panel has concluded that the execution of the removal order should be stayed for a period of five years. CONCLUSION
 The removal order is valid in law. The execution of the removal order is stayed for a period of five years on terms and conditions. ORDER
